mcqs.question: A function runs an O(n) pass over an array, then an O(n²) pass over the same array. What is the function's overall complexity?
options: O(n)
O(n²)
O(n³)
O(n log n)
mcqs.explanation: Sequential blocks add, and Big-O keeps only the fastest-growing term — O(n) + O(n²) simplifies to O(n²) because the quadratic term dominates for large n. It doesn't multiply the two blocks together (that would only happen if the second pass ran once per iteration of the first).

mcqs.question: A function's `if` branch is O(n) and its `else` branch is O(n log n). What is the function's worst-case complexity?
options: O(n), since the if branch is more common
The average of the two, O(n log n / 2)
It depends on which branch the caller intends to hit
O(n log n) — analysis takes the more expensive branch
mcqs.explanation: Worst-case analysis takes the most expensive branch a conditional can reach, never an average or the "typical" path — some inputs will take the O(n log n) branch, so that's the guarantee. Reporting the cheaper branch's cost understates the true worst case.

mcqs.question: A loop runs n times, and each iteration calls `x in some_list` where `some_list` has m elements. What is the total complexity?
options: O(n·m)
O(n), since each call is a single line
O(n + m)
O(m), since the list size doesn't depend on the loop
mcqs.explanation: A called function's own cost multiplies into the loop, exactly like a nested loop would — an O(m) membership check run n times is O(n·m), not O(n). Treating a one-line call as automatically O(1) is the hidden-cost trap this rule exists to catch.

mcqs.question: Why is calling `list.pop(0)` inside an n-iteration loop typically O(n²) overall rather than O(n)?
options: Because `pop(0)` triggers a full re-sort of the list each time
Because `pop(0)` itself is O(n) — every remaining element shifts left to stay contiguous — so n calls cost O(n²)
Because Python lists cannot remove elements from index 0
Because the loop condition re-evaluates the list's length on every iteration
mcqs.explanation: Removing from the front of a contiguous array forces every remaining element to shift down by one slot, which is O(n) per call — unlike `pop()` from the end, which touches nothing else. Called n times inside a loop, that hidden O(n) cost compounds to O(n²).

mcqs.question: Rewriting a loop's `if x in some_list:` as `if x in some_set:` changes the loop's complexity from O(n²) to O(n). Why?
options: Sets are always stored in sorted order, enabling binary search
Set membership hashes the key and probes a bucket in O(1) average, versus scanning the list in O(n)
Sets remove duplicate elements before the check runs
The set version skips checking every element in the loop
mcqs.explanation: A set's membership check hashes the key to a bucket index directly, costing O(1) on average, while a list's `in` scans element by element until it finds a match or reaches the end. The syntax looks identical at the call site, which is exactly why the cost difference is easy to miss.

mcqs.question: A `while` loop divides a variable `x` by 10 each iteration until it reaches 0. What is the loop's complexity in terms of x?
options: O(x), one iteration per unit of x
O(log₁₀ x), since x shrinks by a constant factor each iteration
O(1), since the loop body has no nested loop
mcqs.explanation: Repeatedly dividing by a constant factor is the code shape that produces a logarithm — the iteration count is bounded by how many times you can divide x by 10 before it hits 0, which is log₁₀ x. Reading the loop as "runs over x" and guessing O(x) overstates the cost by an exponential factor.
